why: The brief says outright that commit 3 is 'design work': the store's header and the platform's KaizenSiteHeader take different inputs, and the model must choose how the kept routes (sign-up, themes, status, docs) look and what they lose. Commit 4 moves 43 importers of platform-navigation.ts onto a new reader whose shape it designs, plus a migration copying the theme pages. Commit 2 decides from production evidence whether media rows need a migration. Commit 8 deletes production data for good behind a dump the owner must approve. Only commit 1, an inventory script with a ratchet test, is safe alone, and classifying its entries harms nothing if slightly off.
harm_if_wrong: kaizenaflow.com's pages, theme store or sign-up could lose their header, footer, media or addresses, and in the last push the site's null-store rows (or a template's or support row by a loose WHERE) could be deleted from production.
make_it_cheaper: Split it: commit 1 alone as a cheap step; commit 5 (deleting the 20 pages, with the proxy fallback edit written as code) and commit 6 as cheap-then-review steps once commits 3 and 4 are done; keep 3, 4, 7 and 8 for the stronger model with the owner reading the dump.
brief_problems: done_when's 'rg -l platform_theme_installs … prints 0' cannot hold until the dropping push (src/db/schema.ts names the table); the brief admits this only in checked_in_code, while commit 7's check filters schema.ts out.

Commit 2 asks the cheap model to run site-compare against production and keep before.json outside the repo across later commits and deploys; a fresh session for a later commit will not have that file.
Commit 3's check names src/lib/platform-chrome.scan.test.ts and house-routing.scan.test.ts 'only if step 2.43 is done', so the right names are left to the model.
